sysd-scale-080.title: Database partitioning: cutting a big database into independent pieces
sysd-scale-080.text: A query that touches only one partition runs on that partition's node and nowhere else, so throughput grows linearly as nodes are added. That is the promise of database partitioning: deliberately breaking a large database into smaller, independent parts. Each record, row or document belongs to exactly one partition, so each partition is effectively a small database of its own. It is normally done for manageability, performance, availability or load balancing. More complex queries can be parallelized across nodes, with extra challenges. Partitioning is often combined with replication: a record belongs to one partition but exists on several nodes, and a node can lead some partitions while following others. Systems name the pieces differently: shard in MongoDB, region in HBase, vnode in Cassandra, tablet in {{ref:sysd-scale-038}}. None of this is a {{ref:sysd-scale-142}}, which is a fault in the network between nodes.

sysd-scale-082.title: How a database decides which partition holds a row
sysd-scale-082.text:
Every row needs an address, and the partitioning key supplies it. A relational database takes that key and applies a criterion: range, list, composite, round-robin or {{ref:sysd-scale-084}}. In {{ref:sysd-scale-083}}, continuous ranges of the key go to each partition. List partitioning gives each partition a list of values. Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Denmark, for example, can form a partition for the Nordic countries. Composite partitioning combines schemes, such as range first and then hash. Round-robin partitioning sends the ith tuple in insertion order to partition (i mod n). That gives uniform distribution and parallel sequential access, but reaching tuples by a predicate means accessing the entire relation.

Sharded systems add a few names for the same ideas. The sharding key is a column of the table, and the sharding algorithm uses it to decide which shard stores each row. Choosing the right key and algorithm is crucial for even distribution and performance. Directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table, the directory, that maps keys to shard locations, and routes data by consulting it. Hash-based sharding has an extension in {{ref:sysd-scale-078}}, which moves less data when shards change. It can be seen as a composite of hash and list partitioning. Virtual bucket sharding maps data to virtual buckets and buckets to physical shards. That eases rebalancing without much data movement. When shards follow a real-world segmentation, such as European versus American customers, the right shard is easy to infer and only that shard is queried.

sysd-scale-083.title: Range partitioning: one volume of keys per partition
sysd-scale-083.text: Because the range boundaries are known, a request can be routed straight to the partition that holds its key. That is the appeal of range partitioning, which assigns continuous ranges of the partitioning key to partitions, like the volumes of an encyclopedia. A typical example is a partition for all rows whose zipcode column has a value between 70000 and 79999. Ranges must be contiguous but not overlapping, and key values at or above a range's upper bound go to the next partition. It works on ordered columns such as integers, longs or timestamps. Examples are customers by the alphabetical order of last name, transactions by date range, or user IDs 1 to 1000 in shard 1. Boundaries can be set manually or automatically so that the data is balanced across partitions. Range scans are efficient, but some access patterns, such as writing time-ordered keys, pile load onto one partition, a problem named in {{ref:sysd-scale-081}}.

sysd-scale-085.title: Horizontal partitioning: same columns, fewer rows per table
sysd-scale-085.text: Customers with ZIP codes below 50000 go in a table called CustomersEast, and those at 50000 or above in CustomersWest. That is horizontal partitioning: different rows of a table go into different tables. A view with a union over both tables gives the complete picture of all customers. Holding fewer rows in each table reduces index size, which generally improves search performance. It pays off when there is an obvious, robust and implicit way to tell which partition holds a row without searching the index, as a ZIP code does. Many guides treat the term as a synonym for sharding.

sysd-scale-087.title: Database sharding: spreading one database across many servers
sysd-scale-087.text:
Each shard is the single source for its subset of the data. A database shard is a horizontal partition of the data in a database or search engine. Each may be held on a separate database server instance. Every shard has the same schema and columns but holds a unique, independent subset of the data, and all the shards together contain all of it. Placing them on separate hardware spreads a database across many machines, which can significantly improve performance.

Splitting tables over servers reduces the rows per table and the index size, which generally improves search. The search load then spreads over multiple servers, rather than only over several indexes on one server. That separates sharding from plain {{ref:sysd-scale-085}}, which stays within one schema instance and server. Sharding partitions the table the same way across potentially multiple instances of the schema. Large partitionable tables are distributed across servers, while smaller tables are replicated in full on each server. A mechanism is then needed to keep the replicated tables synchronized.

Sharding relates to {{ref:sysd-scale-141}}, since each shard can sit in its own schema instance, server, data center or region, and it aims to minimize cross-shard access. The sharding logic can live in the application, in a middleware layer between the application and the database, or in the database system itself. Shards also give logical independence. Each can be managed on its own for availability, and sensitive and non-sensitive data can be kept in different partitions for better manageability and security.

sysd-scale-141.title: Shared nothing: every request served by a single node
sysd-scale-141.text: In a shared-nothing system, no two nodes compete for the same memory or storage. A shared-nothing architecture is a distributed computing architecture in which each update request is satisfied by a single node in a cluster. A node here is a processor, memory and storage unit. The intent is to eliminate contention among nodes. Shared everything, by contrast, satisfies requests with arbitrary combinations of nodes and so risks contention when several nodes update the same data at once. Shared-nothing removes single points of failure, so the system keeps running despite node failures, and nodes can upgrade hardware or software without a system-wide shutdown. It scales simply by adding nodes, because no central resource is a bottleneck. Data is typically partitioned among many nodes, and in a database the part on one node is a shard. Commonly used but rarely modified data can be replicated across nodes so more requests resolve on a single node. The weak point is any request that needs data from multiple nodes, which can dramatically reduce throughput.

sysd-scale-081.title: Skew and hot spots: one partition carries the load
sysd-scale-081.text: With ideal distribution, ten nodes process ten times the data and throughput of one node. Skew eats into that. It is the uneven distribution of data or load across partitions, and a partition that receives excessive load is called a hot spot. A sensor network keyed by timestamp shows how it happens: writes concentrate in the partition for the current time period. Prefixing the timestamp with the sensor identifier in a compound key spreads that load. Other remedies are assigning records to nodes at random, at the cost of harder retrieval, key-range partitioning with optimized boundaries, or hash-based partitioning for even load.

sysd-scale-088.title: What sharding costs: harder queries and more to go wrong
sysd-scale-088.text: Sharding buys scale with complexity, in the database infrastructure and in the application code. Developers may need to write more complex SQL queries to handle the sharding logic. Joins that span several shards are often not feasible or not efficient, because the data must be retrieved from multiple servers, and transactions across shards may need {{ref:sysd-scale-001}}. The ORDER BY operation gets more complicated: data is usually fetched from different shards and sorted in the application's code. The software that partitions, balances, coordinates and keeps the data correct can itself fail or introduce errors. Corruption or failure of one shard can affect the integrity of the entire dataset, and fail-over servers must maintain copies of all shards. Backing up the individual shards must be coordinated, and adding indexes, modifying columns or altering the schema all become harder. Uneven distribution, also called a hotspot, forces rebalancing, and changing the sharding scheme after the database is sharded is complex and time-consuming.

sysd-scale-084.title: Hash partitioning: trading range queries for an even load
sysd-scale-084.text: Run a key through a hash function and its neighbors scatter. That is both the strength and the cost of hash partitioning, which turns skewed data into a uniform distribution so that load spreads evenly across partitions. It effectively prevents hot spots, but it sacrifices range query efficiency, because adjacent keys land on different partitions. A shard key such as a customer ID or transaction ID is hashed, which tends to spread data more evenly than range-based sharding. A proper hash function is needed to avoid collisions. Cassandra and MongoDB commonly use MD5. Cassandra also combines both approaches with compound primary keys: the first component is hashed to pick the partition, while the remaining components keep sort order within it. The simplest form is shard_id = hash(user_id) % num_shards, but adding or removing database servers then becomes expensive. That is the problem {{ref:sysd-scale-078}} solves.

sysd-scale-078.title: Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything
sysd-scale-078.text:
Add one server to a pool, and an ordinary hash table remaps nearly all of its keys. The key-to-slot mapping is a modulo operation, so changing the number of slots, here the servers, reshuffles almost everything, and reassigning everything is expensive. Consistent hashing is the fix. It is a technique that lets a hash table be resized while remapping only about n/m keys on average. Here n is the number of keys and m the number of slots.

It hashes both the keys and the servers onto a circle, and assigns each key to the next server found clockwise from it. When a server fails or is added, only the keys next to it on the circle move. Adding the nth server relocates only a 1/n fraction of the keys. Karger and colleagues introduced it in 1997 as the basis of caching protocols that relieve hot spots on very large networks such as the Internet. A consistent hash function changes minimally as its range changes. Those protocols therefore need no current, or even consistent, view of the whole network and scale gracefully as it grows.

In practice it spreads cache keys evenly across shards even if some fail. DynamoDB and Cassandra use it to minimize data movement during rebalancing, and CDNs use it to spread content over edge servers. To stay available and durable, it replicates each data item on N nodes, where N is the replication factor. In eventually consistent systems, the subject of {{ref:sysd-scale-097}}, the copies are made asynchronously. It is not perfect. In theory it spreads load evenly, but in practice load is often uneven and one server can become a hotspot. It also adds complexity, risks one failure triggering others in a chain, and makes key management costly when nodes transiently fail.

sysd-scale-139.title: Distributed hash tables: a lookup service with no center
sysd-scale-139.text: In a distributed hash table, any node can find the value for any key, and no central coordinator is needed. A distributed hash table (DHT) is a distributed system that provides a lookup service similar to a hash table, with key-value pairs stored across the participating nodes. Most DHTs map keys to nodes with {{ref:sysd-scale-078}} or {{ref:sysd-scale-079}}. Adding or removing a node then changes only the keys of adjacent IDs, whereas a traditional hash table remaps nearly the whole keyspace. A DHT has three parts. An abstract keyspace, such as 160-bit strings, comes first. A scheme then splits ownership of it among nodes, and an overlay network lets nodes find the owner of any key. Each node links to a few others, and a lookup is forwarded greedily to the closest neighbor, called key-based routing. A common design has O(log n) neighbors and O(log n) route length, as in {{ref:sysd-scale-140}}, Kademlia and Pastry. DHTs underpin distributed file systems and peer-to-peer file sharing, as in BitTorrent's distributed tracker and IPFS.

sysd-scale-079.title: Rendezvous hashing: every client picks the same server alone
sysd-scale-079.text: Many clients, no coordinator, one answer: that is the point of rendezvous hashing, also called highest random weight (HRW) hashing, designed in 1996. It lets clients reach distributed agreement on a set of k options out of a possible set of n options. A typical use is agreeing on which sites, meaning servers or proxies, an object is assigned to. Each client chooses independently, yet all must pick the same sites, and the standard case is k = 1. All clients share a hash function h. For an object O, each computes the weight h(O, S) for every site S and picks the site with the highest weight. When a site fails, only its objects move, to the next largest weight, while a plain table of n sites would remap every object. Compared with {{ref:sysd-scale-078}}, it is much simpler, needs no precomputed or stored tokens, and handles any k < n. It is now preferred over consistent hashing in many applications, such as the GitHub load balancer, Apache Ignite, {{ref:sysd-msg-036}} and the Twitter EventBus pub/sub platform.

sysd-scale-089.title: Virtual nodes: giving each server many places on the ring
sysd-scale-089.text: Servers are not spread uniformly around a hash ring, so some own more of it than others, which causes skew among nodes. A virtual node, or vnode, is an existing physical node mapped multiple times across the ring. Its share of the key space is then made of several small ranges. The number of duplicate labels a server gets is its weight. Without them, a failed server's keys all move to the next server clockwise, potentially doubling its load. With several positions, its keys go to different servers and spread more evenly. Virtual nodes also speed up rebalancing and lower the probability of hotspots.

sysd-scale-140.title: Chord: finding the node that stores a key
sysd-scale-140.text: Chord supports one operation: given a key, it maps the key onto a node. This distributed lookup protocol lets peer-to-peer applications locate the node storing a data item. Data location is built on top, by storing each key and item at the node the key maps to. Chord uses consistent hashing: nodes are points on a circle, and the keyspace is split into contiguous segments whose endpoints are node identifiers. It adapts efficiently as nodes join and leave, and it answers queries even as the system keeps changing. Theory, simulation and experiments show that its communication cost and per-node state both grow logarithmically with the number of nodes.

sysd-scale-086.title: Vertical partitioning: splitting a table by its columns
sysd-scale-086.text: Horizontal partitioning splits a table by rows; vertical partitioning splits it by columns. It creates tables with fewer columns and stores the remaining columns in additional tables, which is why it is also called row splitting. It goes beyond normalization, splitting columns even in an already normalized table. Infrequently used or very wide columns can be moved to a different machine. A common form separates static from dynamic data, since the static part is faster to access. A view across the two tables restores the original table at a performance penalty. A columnar database can be seen as one vertically partitioned until each column has its own table.

sysd-scale-091.title: Federation: many databases that look like one
sysd-scale-091.text: Federation, also called functional partitioning, splits up databases by function and then presents the pieces as a whole. A federation makes several distinct physical databases appear as one logical database to end users. Federated schemas tie them together, expressing the commonality of data and specifying what the components may share. The result is a cohesive, unified view of data from multiple sources, which can include databases and other structured and unstructured data. A federated database is transparent, so users need not know where data is stored. It copes with differing hardware, protocols and data models, and it leaves existing data sources and their interfaces unchanged. The advantages are flexible data sharing, autonomy among components, unified access to heterogeneous data, and no tight coupling of applications with legacy databases. The disadvantages are extra hardware and complexity, complex joins of data from two databases, dependence on autonomous data sources, and limits on query performance and scalability.

sysd-scale-090.title: When sharding is worth it, and when it is not
sysd-scale-090.text: The first rule of sharding is to try everything else first. It is generally recommended only when other optimization strategies have proven insufficient, because sharding a table before optimizing it locally adds needless complexity. The costs are listed in {{ref:sysd-scale-088}}. The case for it is a single server holding too much data, serving too many requests, or answering ever more slowly as data grows. After a certain point it is cheaper and more feasible to scale horizontally by adding machines than vertically by buying more powerful servers. Singh adds using existing hardware instead of high-end machines, and scaling quickly by adding shards.

openers.sharding-and-partitioning: Which piece of the data lives where? That one question drives this chapter. A partition is a division of a logical database into distinct, independent parts, and a shard is a horizontal partition that may sit on its own database server. The rules for assigning data range from key ranges, like the volumes of an encyclopedia, to hash functions that turn skewed data into a uniform distribution, with refinements such as consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing. Sharding also has a price: skew and hot spots, and more complexity in the infrastructure and the application code.

reviews.sharding-and-partitioning: Every scheme in this chapter answers the same question, which piece of the data lives where, with a rule applied to a partitioning key. Range partitioning keeps neighbors together, hash partitioning spreads load evenly, and each pays for it in skew or in range queries. Sharding puts the pieces on separate servers in a shared-nothing design, at the cost of harder queries, harder joins and rebalancing. Consistent hashing, rendezvous hashing and virtual nodes keep the data that moves small when servers come and go, and distributed hash tables such as Chord use the same idea with no central coordination. Because of those costs, sharding is recommended only when other optimizations have proven insufficient.
